newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary committee meets on single currency.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary committee meets on single currency.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee began a two-day meeting on Monday to discuss a budget stability pact for countries joining a future economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We have a full agenda since we haven't met for two months," said one official ahead of this afternoon's gathering.
The group, comprising national treasury and central bank officials, will also focus on a post-EMU exchange rate grid, linking the single currency to those not in the core group.

Also on the agenda is the legal framework for the single currency, an issue of particular relevance to those worried about the continuity of financial contracts after the EMU's expected launch in 1999.
"It's the same work that we're continuing with with...preparations for Dublin," said another official.
The decisions reached by the monetary committee will be forwarded to an informal meeting of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin on September 21.

Regarding the stability pact, EU monetary officials believe that an accord to enforce budgetary discipline among countries inside EMU will be the hardest challenge among the three items up for discussion.
Several said they did not expect all of the outstanding issue on such a pact to be resolved at this meeting, with some anticipating a mandate for a compromise by December.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the primary catalyst behind a budget stability pact, has argued that sanctions on countries running excessive deficits should be automatic.

The problem so far is how to agree on a formula that makes the EU's current excessive deficits procedure more swift and punitive. But there are limits to how far they can go given the strictures of the Maastricht treaty.
A separate issue concerns the period from when a country is deemed to have an excessive deficit to when it must put forward a plan to rectify it.

EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault De Silguy said last week that the shortest possible time frame would be nine months, with most countries divided over whether it could be as long as 12 months.
For example, the decision on whether a government had an excessive deficit would be made in March of the following year once reliable data is available.
The offending government would then have until December to put forward a plan to bring its finances under control. If the plan was considered not credible the government could be fined.
Separately, officials played down the possibility that the monetary committee would decide to put the Finnish markka into the ERM on either Monday or Tuesday.
Even though the gathering offers them an ideal opportunity for a surprise announcement, decisions on ERM participation are traditionally taken over the weekend, officials said.
